lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Maximum Value Search
task: A brute force algorithmic strategy evaluates every candidate within a dataset to ensure the correct solution is identified.
To find the maximum value, the algorithm must systematically check every element against a recorded state.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `find_max(arr)`.
2. Implement a defensive check: if the array is empty, return the string 'Error'.
3. Initialize a tracking variable and assign it the value located at the first index.
4. Construct an iterative loop to traverse every element in the array.
5. Within the loop, evaluate if the current element exceeds your recorded maximum.
6. If true, update your tracking variable to equal the current element.
7. Return the tracking variable.

lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Minimum Value Search
task: Finding the minimum value within an unsorted array requires the identical O(n) sequential traversal strategy, utilizing an inverted logical comparison.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `find_min(arr)`.
2. Evaluate if the list is empty, returning 'Error' if true.
3. Initialize a variable to track the minimum value, seeding it with the first element.
4. Construct a loop to traverse the array.
5. Evaluate if the current item is strictly less than your tracked minimum. If true, update the tracking variable.
6. Return the tracking variable.

lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Target Sum Search
task: A brute force target sum algorithm checks every possible combination of two elements to determine if they accumulate to a specific value.
Because this requires an inner loop to evaluate subsequent elements for every outer loop iteration, the time complexity scales quadratically.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `sum_search(arr, target)`.
2. Construct an outer loop iterating from 0 to the length of the array minus 1.
3. Construct an inner loop starting from the element immediately following the outer loop's index, up to the end of the array.
4. Inside the inner loop, evaluate if the sum of the elements at both pointers equals the target.
5. If true, return a list containing both elements.
6. If all combinations are evaluated without a match, return an empty list.

lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Conditional Counting
task: Exhaustive search can be combined with conditional logic to aggregate specific data subsets, such as computing the total number of even integers within an array.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `count_evens(arr)`.
2. Initialize an accumulator variable to track the count.
3. Construct a standard traversal loop over the array.
4. Within the loop, evaluate if the current element is an even number by checking if it is cleanly divisible by 2 using the modulo operator.
5. If the condition evaluates to true, increment the accumulator variable by 1.
6. Return the accumulator variable.

lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Early Exit Optimization
task: When an algorithm only requires the first valid instance of a condition, executing the loop to completion is inefficient.
Implementing an early exit optimizes the average-case time complexity, although the worst-case remains O(n).
Instructions:
1. Define the function `first_negative(arr)`.
2. Construct a linear traversal loop over the array.
3. Evaluate if the current item is strictly less than 0.
4. If true, return the item immediately to terminate the execution.
5. If the traversal concludes without encountering a negative number, return `0`.

lesson_2.title: Linear Search: Target Identification
task: Linear Search relies on evaluating elements sequentially to locate a specific target within an unsorted dataset.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `linear_search(arr, target)`.
2. Construct an indexed loop from 0 up to the length of the array.
3. Inside the loop, evaluate if the element at the current index equals the target.
4. If the condition evaluates to true, return the index variable immediately.
5. If the loop completes without identifying the target, return `-1`.

lesson_2.title: Linear Search: Frequency Counting
task: Rather than terminating upon the first identification, a full linear traversal can be utilized to compute the frequency of a target value within the dataset.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `count_occurrences(arr, target)`.
2. Initialize an accumulator variable to track the frequency count.
3. Construct a standard traversal loop over the array.
4. Evaluate if the current element equals the target. If true, increment your accumulator variable by 1.
5. Return the finalized accumulator variable.

lesson_2.title: Linear Search: Reverse Traversal
task: To locate the final occurrence of a specific target, traversing the array from index 0 to the end is mathematically inefficient.
Implementing a reverse traversal ensures the first match encountered is the last occurrence in the sequence, allowing for an immediate early exit.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `last_occurrence(arr, target)`.
2. Construct a loop that iterates backward, starting the index at the final valid array position and decrementing to 0.
3. Inside the loop, evaluate if the element at the current index equals the target.
4. If true, execute an immediate return of the current index.
5. If the loop concludes without a match, return `-1`.

lesson_2.title: Linear Search: Bounded Range
task: Search algorithms frequently operate within dynamic subsections of memory defined by `start` and `end` pointers.
Accepting dynamic bounds without validation presents a critical stability risk. The bounds must be sanitized prior to execution.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `search_in_range(arr, target, start, end)`.
2. Apply boundary validation: prevent negative bounds by clamping the start pointer to 0 if necessary.
3. Apply upper boundary validation: clamp the end pointer to the final valid index to prevent overflow.
4. Construct an indexed loop originating at the validated `start` parameter and terminating at `end`.
5. Evaluate if the element at the current index matches the target. Return the index if true.
6. Return `-1` if the bounded search completes without a match.

lesson_2.title: Linear Search: Multi-Target Extraction
task: When an algorithm must identify multiple occurrences of a target and preserve their locations, it requires an out-of-place allocation strategy.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `multi_search(arr, target)`.
2. Initialize an empty array to warehouse the identified indices.
3. Construct an indexed loop traversing the length of the array.
4. Evaluate if the element at the current index equals the target. If true, append the index to the auxiliary array.
5. Return the auxiliary array upon completion.

lesson_3.title: Bubble Sort: Ascending Execution
task: Bubble Sort operates by systematically comparing adjacent elements and exchanging them if they violate the intended sequence order.
This algorithm relies on nested iteration, resulting in an O(n²) time complexity.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `bubble_sort_asc(arr)`.
2. Construct an outer loop encompassing the entire array to track the sorting passes.
3. Construct an inner loop to traverse the unsorted boundary.
4. Evaluate adjacent elements: if the current element is strictly greater than the subsequent element, execute an in-place swap.
5. Return the sorted array structure.

lesson_3.title: Selection Sort: Ascending Execution
task: Selection Sort divides the array into sorted and unsorted segments. It scans the unsorted segment to locate the minimum element and swaps it into the sorted boundary.
This requires pointer indirection: tracking the structural index of the minimum value rather than the integer itself.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `selection_sort(arr)`.
2. Construct an outer loop tracking the boundary of the sorted subsection.
3. Initialize a variable to track the index of the minimum value, setting it initially to the outer loop's position.
4. Construct an inner loop to scan the remaining unsorted elements.
5. Evaluate if the current unsorted element is less than the element at your tracked minimum index. If true, update your minimum index pointer.
6. Execute an in-place swap to move the absolute minimum value into the sorted boundary.
7. Return the sorted array.

lesson_3.title: Bubble Sort: Descending Execution
task: To sequence elements in descending order, the algorithmic structure remains identical while the adjacent evaluation logic is inverted.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `bubble_sort_desc(arr)`.
2. Implement the nested iterative structure established in the previous Bubble Sort exercise.
3. Modify the conditional evaluation: if the current element is strictly less than the subsequent element, execute the in-place swap.
4. Return the sorted array.

lesson_3.title: Selection Sort: Descending Execution
task: Selection Sort can be inverted by searching the unsorted boundary for the maximum value rather than the minimum.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `selection_sort_desc(arr)`.
2. Implement the nested iterative structure. Initialize a tracker for the maximum index rather than the minimum.
3. Modify the conditional evaluation: if the current unsorted element exceeds the element at your tracked maximum index, update the pointer.
4. Execute an in-place swap to lock the maximum value into the sorted boundary.
5. Return the sorted array.

lesson_3.title: Sort Execution Tracking: Single Pass
task: To isolate and understand the underlying mechanics of Bubble Sort, we can track the structural state of the array after executing a single complete traversal.
A single pass of the adjacent comparison logic guarantees that the maximum element is pushed to the highest available index.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `single_pass(arr)`.
2. Construct a single sequential loop that traverses the unsorted boundary.
3. Evaluate adjacent logic: if the current element is greater than the subsequent element, execute an in-place swap.
4. Return the modified array.
5. Observe that isolating the primary sorting mechanism reduces the execution to O(n) linear time.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Two-Pointer Convergence
task: Evaluating every possible pair using nested loops to locate a target sum enforces an O(n²) time complexity.
If the underlying array is guaranteed to be strictly sorted, the algorithm can be optimized to O(n) linear time utilizing converging pointers.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Remove the nested loops entirely. Initialize two boundary variables: `left` pointing to the first index, and `right` pointing to the final index.
2. Construct a single `while` loop that executes as long as the pointers have not crossed.
3. Inside the loop, compute the combined sum of the elements currently located at the `left` and `right` pointers.
4. If the combined sum equals the target, return the two elements in a new list.
5. Pointer logic: If the combined sum is strictly less than the target, advance the left pointer forward to increase the sum.
6. If the combined sum is strictly greater than the target, decrement the right pointer backward to decrease the sum.
7. Return an empty list if the traversal concludes without identifying a match.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Center Index Verification
task: The previous brute force algorithm utilized nested loop iteration to identify a majority element, resulting in an O(n²) time complexity.
If the input array is strictly sorted, the required algorithmic evaluation reduces to O(1) constant time.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Remove all iterative loop constructs from the execution space.
2. By mathematical definition, if an element comprises more than half of a strictly sorted array, it must occupy the exact center position.
3. Compute the exact middle index of the array utilizing the integer division operator.
4. Access and return the element at the computed middle index.
5. Observe the analyzer verify the optimization from O(n²) exhaustive search to O(1) constant-time lookup.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Pre-Sorting for Adjacency
task: Evaluating every possible pair to verify duplicates via nested loops dictates an O(n²) time complexity.
This algorithm can be mathematically optimized to O(n log n). Sorting the array forces identical values into adjacent positions, enabling verification through a single linear scan.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Remove the nested loop structure entirely.
2. Execute an in-place sort operation on the array. This structural mutation incurs an O(n log n) time complexity.
3. Construct a single sequential loop iterating through the array. Ensure you stop one element early to prevent out-of-bounds evaluation.
4. Evaluate sequential adjacency: check if the current element is strictly equal to the element immediately following it.
5. If equality is confirmed, return `True` immediately.
6. Return `False` if the scan completes without detecting identical neighboring elements.
